title: On Carriedo Street, Henry Sy Chose a Shop Name He Could Repeat
dek: In 1958, after a decade of small shoe shops in downtown Manila, Henry Sy opened Shoemart with a name built to be used again.

story.event: Opening the first Shoemart shoe store on Carriedo Street, Quiapo
story.summary: Henry Sy, who came to Manila from Fujian at 12 and lost his family's shops in the Second World War, started selling shoes after the war and ran three shoe stores on Carriedo Street from 1946 to 1948. In October 1958 he opened Shoemart there, choosing a name he could reuse for every branch. Shoemart opened in Cubao and Makati in 1960, became SM in 1972 and grew into the Philippines' largest retail group.
paragraphs: In October 1958 a shoe shop called Shoemart opened on Carriedo Street in Quiapo, then the busy centre of downtown Manila. It was not Henry Sy's first. Since the end of the war he had opened three shoe stores on the same street, named Plaza, Paris and Park Avenue. This time he wanted a name that could travel. "I did not want to have to think of a new name each time I would open a new store," he said in 2009. The next could simply be Shoemart Cubao, or Shoemart Makati.

Sy had come from Fujian province in 1936, aged 12, imagining a better life because his father sent money home. Instead, he recalled, his father kept a small sari-sari store, a neighbourhood shop, along Carriedo, and the boy helped out. The war took almost everything: one of the family's stores burned and another was looted, and his father returned to China while Henry stayed. Goods were scarce afterwards and everyone, he said, was buying and selling. He chose shoes "because I thought everyone would need a pair of shoes," and began with surplus American army boots.

What he wanted from the business, by his own account, was modest: a steady income for his family. He kept his father's frugal habits, paying himself a salary and putting the profits back into the shops, and he said the capital was internally generated, which eased the pressure in bad times; Chinabank's history records that it also gave him a credit line of 1 million pesos in 1949. Shoemart was air-conditioned, which Bloomberg described as a first for a Philippine shoe shop. He thought, the Inquirer reported, that if he could sell a pair of shoes to every Filipino he would be a successful man.

The name did its job. In 1960 Shoemart opened in Cubao and Makati. Shoe manufacturers could not keep up with the volumes he wanted, so after six shoe stores he moved into clothing and other goods. In 1972, under martial law, he opened his first department store in Quiapo, and Shoemart became SM. His first mall, SM City North EDSA, followed in 1985. When he died in January 2019, aged 94, he was the richest person in the Philippines.

quote.text: 'Not so,' says the good Heaven; 'plod and plough, vamp your old coats and hats, weave a shoestring; great affairs and the best wine by and by.'
quote.source_title: The Conduct of Life, Project Gutenberg eBook #39827
quote.connection: Emerson imagines someone begging the gods for a great task. Heaven refuses and hands over small work instead: mend the coat, weave the shoestring, and let great affairs come later. Sy spent twelve years on corner shoe shops before Shoemart, and the malls came decades after that.

reflection: What stands out about Shoemart in 1958 is how ordinary it was. Sy had already run shoe shops for a decade, and his stated aim was a steady income for his family. The one new thing was a name built to be used again. He did not need to foresee malls to leave room for a second shop.

You can do something similar without a grand plan. Some of your work is a one-off, and some of it you will do again and again: a form, a checklist, a way of explaining things to someone new. Giving that work a plain name and a shape it can be reused in is a small kindness to the person you will be next month.
invitation: Pick one task you have done more than twice this month. Give it a plain name and write its steps on a single page, so that next time you do not start from nothing.

sources.title: Philippines' richest man Henry Sy, who started as a shoe seller, dies aged 94
sources.supports: Died on 19 January 2019 aged 94, the richest person in the Philippines; came to the Philippines at 12 and worked in his father's Manila store from 1936; the store burned and looted in the war; after the war sold shoes imported by US soldiers and set up a footwear store; founded ShoeMart in 1958, the first air-conditioned shop to sell shoes in the Philippines; after six shoe stores diversified because shoe manufacturers could not meet his volumes; first department store in 1972; first mall in 1985

research_notes: Founding date of the shoe business: Sy's own 2009 account (Inquirer) gives three Carriedo stores, Plaza (1946), Paris (1947) and Park Avenue (1948), before Shoemart in 1958; Tsinoy also dates his first Quiapo shoe store to 1946; the Bloomberg obituary (Straits Times) says the company 'started as a shoe store in 1948'. The story follows Sy's own dates and treats 1958 as the opening of the first store under the Shoemart name, which Rappler dates to October 1958. AFP (2008) says he 'started off selling shoes to American GIs in 1958', which conflates the surplus-boot trade with Shoemart and is not used. Birthplace is given variously as Xiamen (Bloomberg, Tsinoy, Town & Country Philippines) and Jinjiang (other obituaries); the story says only Fujian province, as Sy himself did. War losses: Sy says one family store burned and another was looted; Bloomberg says the store was burned and looted; Rappler (2024) says it burned in 1942 under the Japanese occupation; the story uses Sy's version without a year. Father's shop: Sy places it on Carriedo; Town & Country Philippines (2018) says Echague Street; the story follows Sy. Town & Country's 2018 'Shoemart facts' piece (surplus G.I. boots, looking abroad for shoes) was read but is not cited because neither the live page nor its archived copy loads for the verifier; the story therefore gives the Bloomberg reason for diversifying (manufacturers could not meet his volumes) and does not claim he imported shoes. Funding: Sy said the capital was internally generated and that SM avoided borrowing before its 1995 listing, while Chinabank's histories (via Rappler) record a P1 million credit line in 1949; both are given, and funding is set to 'bootstrapped' because no outside equity is documented before the listings of the 1990s. The 'sell a pair of shoes to every Filipino' line is the Inquirer writer's paraphrase, attributed as such. Sy's quotations come from the Inquirer's 2009 interview. The New York Times obituary loads for the verifier but could not be read here, so it is not cited.
